source.title: Towards Theoretical Understanding of Large Batch Training in Stochastic Gradient Descent

record.tranche_reason: The paper experimentally varies learning-rate-to-batch-size ratios and reports training and test performance, using a different setup from the cited large-batch studies; its theory and experiments also measure loss curvature, but do not directly test the claim versions about generalization-gap measures.
record.gate_note: The paper focuses on the sharp-minimizer part of the large-batch hypothesis. Rows cover the three reported SGD settings' training/test comparison and the reported later test-loss comparison. The sharpness curves are reported only as figure-level findings and do not measure a claim version's specified training-to-test gap or magnitude-aware perturbation measure.
record.test_reason: The study tests learning-rate-to-batch-size effects on SGD geometry and performance, but no listed version directly. Its batches of 128 and 256 are both explicitly classified as small batches, with no demonstrated workload-dependent threshold. Its Hessian measure does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness or ranking of generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Under their SDE assumptions, the authors argue that larger learning-rate-to-batch-size ratios speed movement toward flatter minima and that asymptotic preference for equally valued flatter minima is independent of batch size. Their MNIST experiments also show that the larger ratio can improve training performance while worsening later test loss; they leave further generalization theory for future work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses 4-layer batch-normalized ReLU MLPs on MNIST and varies three learning-rate/batch-size pairs; the study focuses on sharpness dynamics and does not reproduce the cited large-batch benchmarks or fixed-epoch batch-size comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio; test-loss comparison changes over time, with the smaller ratio reported to have smaller test loss after 100 epochs.

fits_no_version.finding: At batch size 128, learning rate 0.1 gives better training performance than 0.01, while 0.01 gives lower test loss after approximately 100 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning-rate choice at a fixed small batch size can trade better training performance for worse later held-out loss.

fits_no_version.finding: The settings 0.1/128 and 0.2/256 have similar training and test errors over 200 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Proportional learning-rate and batch-size scaling can preserve performance across the tested small-batch settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger learning-rate-to-batch-size ratios reach lower Hessian Frobenius norms faster, yet can have worse later test loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Faster convergence toward minima with lower unscaled Hessian norms need not imply better held-out loss.

record.problems: The generalization comparisons are reported through figures without extracted numerical values; the text interprets performance using one experiment for Figure 5 after noting that ten runs were close. The model is an MNIST MLP, and the paper explicitly leaves further theoretical analysis of generalization error for future work.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 reports Hessian Frobenius-norm curves and figure descriptions, but these concern sharpness dynamics rather than a claim version's named generalization-gap measure. Figure 4 reports training accuracy and loss only and was not retained as it does not report test performance.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Held-out penalties beyond a workload-dependent batch-size threshold under fixed epoch budgets, and whether recipe adaptations remove such penalties.
Effects of adding or removing dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its association with training-to-test gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Equal-ratio training and test errors being close means performance is similar across the two settings; it does not assert that training error equals test error. Figure 5 reports one run, justified by similar training curves across ten runs, without numerical uncertainty for held-out performance.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
Large batches beyond a workload-dependent size; fixed epoch budgets across batch sizes; longer training, warmup, normalization, regularization, and other datasets or models.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its ranking of training-to-test gaps against other measures.
Removal of memorized training examples and its effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: 4-layer batch-normalized ReLU MLPs
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD using learning rate 0.01 and batch size 128; reported training and test accuracy/loss.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy and cross entropy loss
rows.value: Figure 5 reports training and test accuracy and loss; text states test loss is smaller after a certain time for this smaller ratio, specifically after 100 epochs.
rows.note: No numerical train-test gap or accuracy/loss values are supplied in the text for this individual setting; the described test-loss comparison is relative to the other ratios.
rows.check: The smaller learning-rate ratio yields lower test loss after 100 epochs, but comparison with R2 holds batch size at 128. This measures a learning-rate effect, not V5's large-batch penalty.

rows.subject: 4-layer batch-normalized ReLU MLPs
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD using learning rate 0.1 and batch size 128; reported training and test accuracy/loss.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy and cross entropy loss
rows.value: Figure 5 reports training and test accuracy and loss; text states this setting has better training accuracy and smaller training loss than the 0.01/128 setting, while the latter has smaller test loss after 100 epochs.
rows.note: No exact numerical train-test gap or test-loss values are stated; the text describes better training performance but worse test loss after the stated time compared with the smaller ratio.
rows.check: Better training performance and worse later test loss relative to R1 arise at the same batch size. The extracted partial state is not evidence of a partial V5 effect.

rows.subject: 4-layer batch-normalized ReLU MLPs
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD using learning rate 0.2 and batch size 256; reported training and test accuracy/loss.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy and cross entropy loss
rows.value: Figure 5 reports training and test accuracy and loss; the text groups this setting with 0.1/128 as having the same learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio and says their training and test errors are very close.
rows.note: No exact values are stated. The paper's claim is that equal ratios yield similar performance, not that this setting differs from another batch size at a fixed epoch budget.
rows.check: Compared with R2, doubling both batch size and learning rate gives similar training and test performance over the same 200 epochs. Neither batch is shown to exceed a workload-dependent threshold; this cannot establish removal of a large-batch penalty.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The three tested MNIST settings at 200 epochs
reader_labels.reason: Training and test errors are described as very close for the equal-ratio settings, while the smaller ratio has smaller test loss after 100 epochs; rows R1–R3 do not establish a general penalty for large batches at fixed epochs.
